Night rules out arm signals.","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F04"]},"result":{"text":"Dana uses her signal lights for both moves and checks ahead, behind and beside her each time.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-R01"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking another driver's blinking signal guarantees where that car will go.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]},"correction":{"text":"The driver may turn the other way or turn without signaling, so you never rely only on a signal.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Signal and look before every move.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You are driving a long moving truck on a bright afternoon and your turn signal bulb has burned out. Can you use your arm instead?","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},"answer":{"text":"No. Hand-and-arm signals are not used while driving a wide or long vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05"]},"rationale":{"text":"Daylight alone is not enough; the size of the vehicle rules out arm signals.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Signals come first","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signal before turns, lane changes and exits.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},{"text":"Moving and curb signals follow different rules.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},{"text":"Arm signals have strict limits.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about telling other road users what you are about to do, and checking that it is safe before you do it. A signal is required before you turn, before you change lanes, before you leave a roundabout and before you pull away from a curb. Each of those moves also comes with a look ahead, behind and to the side. We will cover how early your signal has to go on, how the curb rule differs from the rule for moving traffic, when hand-and-arm signals are allowed, and why another driver's blinker is never something to bet on. These rules are short, but the details are where people slip.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Four moves that need signals","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Turning.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},{"text":"Changing lanes.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},{"text":"Leaving a roundabout.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},{"text":"Pulling away from a curb.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Start with the list, because test questions often hide one of these moves inside a longer story. You signal before turning, whether at an intersection or somewhere else. You signal before changing lanes. You signal before leaving a roundabout, which surprises some drivers who think of the circle as one continuous road. And you signal before you pull away from a curb into traffic. The signal is only half of the job. Before any of these four moves, you also check ahead, behind and to the side to be sure the move is safe. A signal announces your plan; the check confirms the plan will not put anyone in danger.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Moving traffic versus the curb","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Moving: signal at least one hundred feet ahead.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-R02"]},{"text":"Curb: signal long enough to warn drivers.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-R02"]},{"text":"Only the moving rule sets a distance.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two signal timing rules sound alike but work differently. When you are already moving in traffic, your turn signal must go on at least one hundred feet before the turn or the lane change. That is a minimum, so signaling earlier is fine, but later is not. When you are pulling away from a curb, there is no set distance. Instead, you keep the signal on long enough that drivers know you are coming into their lane. So if a question asks about a parked car entering traffic, look for the answer about warning drivers, not the answer about one hundred feet. The distance belongs to moving traffic.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"When arms can signal","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Daylight with a clear view of one thousand feet.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06"]},{"text":"Night or poor visibility: signal lights only.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06"]},{"text":"Never in a wide or long vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06"]},{"text":"Three signals: right, left, stop or slow.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Hand-and-arm signals are a backup with tight limits. You may use them only in daylight, and only when you can clearly see people and vehicles one thousand feet away. At night, or whenever visibility is poor, you must use your signal lights. Signal lights, by contrast, work at any time. There is a second limit that has nothing to do with light: do not use hand-and-arm signals while driving a wide or long vehicle. The manual shows three of these signals, one for a right turn, one for a left turn, and one for stopping or slowing down. If a question offers a hand signal at night, it is the wrong answer.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Blinkers can mislead","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"A signal is a hint, not a promise.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-F01"]},{"text":"The driver may turn the other way.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-F01"]},{"text":"Some drivers turn without signaling.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap that has nothing to do with your own signal. When another driver's turn signal is blinking, it is tempting to plan your move around it, for example pulling out because a car seems about to turn off your path. Never rely only on that signal. The driver may turn the other way, or may turn without signaling at all, so a signal tells you less than it seems. Treat every signal you see as information to weigh, then wait until the car's movement confirms what it is doing. Your own check ahead, behind and to the side is what keeps you safe, not someone else's blinker.","fact_ids":["sec05-F07","sec05-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick check: arm signals","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"A long truck, bright afternoon.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"The signal bulb is out.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F04"]},{"text":"Can you use your arm?","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: imagine you are driving a long moving truck on a bright afternoon, and the turn signal bulb has burned out. Can you use a hand-and-arm signal instead? The answer is no. Daylight and a clear long view are needed for arm signals, but they are not enough on their own. There is a separate rule that you do not use hand-and-arm signals while driving a wide or long vehicle at all. So the size of the vehicle settles it, whatever the light. If you answered yes because it was daytime, go back to the two limits on arm signals: light and visibility, and the vehicle itself.","fact_ids":["sec05-F05","sec05-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Signals in brief","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-R02","sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signal and check before four moves.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-R02","sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},{"text":"Moving: one hundred feet; curb: long enough.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-R02","sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},{"text":"Arms: daylight, long view, ordinary vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-R02","sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, you signal before turning, changing lanes, leaving a roundabout and pulling away from a curb, and before each of those moves you check ahead, behind and to the side. In moving traffic, the signal goes on at least one hundred feet before the move. From a curb, it stays on long enough for drivers to know you are coming. Hand-and-arm signals are for daylight with a clear view of one thousand feet, never at night or in poor visibility, and never in a wide or long vehicle. The three arm signals cover right turns, left turns and stopping or slowing. And never rely only on another driver's signal.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-R02","sec05-F04","sec05-R01","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec05-u02","module_id":"sec05-m02","objective_ids":["sec05-u02"],"title":{"text":"Safe turns, bikes and walkers","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-F22"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Turning rules apply at every turn, and a turn cuts across the paths of bicyclists and pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F12"]},{"text":"The bike lane rule allows one thing and forbids another, which makes it a favorite trick question.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-R03"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Omar wants to turn right into an alley, and a bike lane runs along the curb beside him.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F10"]},"reasoning":{"text":"He checks mirrors and over his shoulder for a rider in his blind spot, and does not pull into the bike lane early.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11","sec05-R03"]},"result":{"text":"With no rider to yield to, he crosses the bike lane during the turn, slowly and smoothly, into the nearest lane of the alley.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-F09","sec05-F22","sec05-F12"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking that if you end up in the wrong lane, a quick swerve at the corner is the safe fix.","fact_ids":["sec05-F13"]},"correction":{"text":"Go on to the next intersection instead; circling the block is safer than a last-second change.","fact_ids":["sec05-F13"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Nearest to nearest, cross the bike lane, never ride it.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-R03"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A bicyclist is coming up the bike lane on your right just as you begin a right turn into a driveway. Who goes first?","fact_ids":["sec05-F12"]},"answer":{"text":"The bicyclist. When turning, you yield to bicyclists in a bike lane or on a sidewalk.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12"]},"rationale":{"text":"Turning rules apply at driveways too, and the rider in the bike lane has priority over your turn.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F08"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Turning without surprises","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Turning rules apply everywhere you turn.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},{"text":"Nearest lane to nearest lane.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},{"text":"Bicyclists and pedestrians come first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"A turn is the moment your car crosses the paths of other people, so the habits around it matter. In this lesson you will see that turning rules apply wherever you turn, not just at intersections. You will learn the general lane rule for every turn, the two turning errors the manual warns about, and exactly what you may and may not do with a bicycle lane. You will also see why a shoulder check matters, who you must yield to while turning, and what to do when you discover you are in the wrong lane for your turn. The common thread is patience: plan early and turn smoothly.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Every turn counts","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Driveways and alleys follow turning rules.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09"]},{"text":"Check behind and beside you early.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09"]},{"text":"Turn smoothly at a lower speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Many drivers think of turning rules as intersection rules, but they apply wherever you turn, including into driveways and alleys. So a turn into a parking lot entrance in the middle of a block carries the same duties as a turn at a corner. The preparation also starts earlier than many people expect. Check for traffic behind you and beside you well before you begin the turn, not as the wheel is already turning. Then make the turn itself smoothly and at a lower speed. A smooth, slower turn gives you time to see a pedestrian or a rider and gives drivers behind you time to react.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Nearest lane to nearest lane","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Start in the nearest lane for your direction.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},{"text":"End in the nearest lane in the new direction.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},{"text":"No swinging wide, no lane changes mid-turn.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"The general turning rule is simple to state. Go from the nearest lane in your direction of travel into the nearest lane in the direction you want to go. Two things break that rule. One is swinging wide, where the car drifts out of its path to make the corner feel easier. The other is changing lanes during the turn. The manual pictures two classic errors that come from ignoring this rule: turning into the wrong lane, and turning from the wrong lane. When a question describes a turn that ends in a far lane, or starts from a lane farther out, it is describing one of those errors.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Bike lanes and your turn","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-R03","sec05-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"You may cross a bike lane to turn.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-R03","sec05-F11"]},{"text":"You must not pull into it to get ready.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-R03","sec05-F11"]},{"text":"Check mirrors and over your shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-R03","sec05-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Bicycle lanes create one of the most tested turning rules. You may cross a bike lane to make a turn. What you must not do is pull into the bike lane ahead of time to get ready for the turn. The difference is between passing across the lane during the turn and driving in it beforehand. Before you turn, check your mirrors and look over your shoulder, because a bicyclist can come up beside you in your blind spot while you are preparing. A rider can arrive in the space you are about to cross while you are still getting set, so that last look over your shoulder is the one that matters.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-R03","sec05-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Who you yield to","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F11","sec05-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Bicyclists in a bike lane or on a sidewalk.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F11","sec05-F09"]},{"text":"Pedestrians in the crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F11","sec05-F09"]},{"text":"Check the crosswalk before you go.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F11","sec05-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Turning never gives you priority over the people around you. When you turn, you must yield to bicyclists in a bike lane, and also to bicyclists riding on a sidewalk, since your turn crosses both paths. You also check the crosswalk you are turning through and stop for pedestrians. A signal does not change this. Even if you signaled early and correctly, a rider in the bike lane or a person in the crosswalk still goes first. Put the checks together: mirrors and shoulder for the rider in your blind spot, then the crosswalk for anyone walking, and only then complete the turn smoothly and at a lower speed.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F11","sec05-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Wrong lane at the corner","fact_ids":["sec05-F13","sec05-F23","sec05-F22"]},"lines":[{"text":"Do not cut across at the last second.","fact_ids":["sec05-F13","sec05-F23","sec05-F22"]},{"text":"Go on to the next intersection.","fact_ids":["sec05-F13","sec05-F23","sec05-F22"]},{"text":"Circling the block is the safer choice.","fact_ids":["sec05-F13","sec05-F23","sec05-F22"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap that tests your judgment more than your memory. You reach an intersection and realize you are in the wrong lane for the turn you wanted. The tempting answer is a quick lane change or a sudden turn from the lane you are in. Both are wrong. Turning from the wrong lane is one of the errors the manual pictures, and a last-second change of lane or direction is riskier than simply going on. The safe choice is to continue to the next intersection and circle the block. You lose a minute, but you keep the general rule intact: nearest lane to nearest lane, with no surprises.","fact_ids":["sec05-F13","sec05-F23","sec05-F22"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick check: driveway turn","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F08","sec05-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"You start a right turn into a driveway.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F08","sec05-F10"]},{"text":"A rider is in the bike lane.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F08","sec05-F10"]},{"text":"Who goes first?","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F08","sec05-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are starting a right turn into a driveway in the middle of a block, and a bicyclist is coming up the bike lane on your right. Second, when you turn you must yield to bicyclists in a bike lane or on a sidewalk. You let the rider pass, then cross the bike lane during your turn without pulling into it beforehand. If you thought the driveway turn was an exception, review where turning rules apply.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F08","sec05-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Turning habits in brief","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-F22","sec05-F23","sec05-F10","sec05-R03","sec05-F11","sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Rules apply at driveways and alleys.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-F22","sec05-F23","sec05-F10","sec05-R03","sec05-F11","sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},{"text":"Cross the bike lane, never pull into it.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-F22","sec05-F23","sec05-F10","sec05-R03","sec05-F11","sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},{"text":"Wrong lane: go on and circle back.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-F22","sec05-F23","sec05-F10","sec05-R03","sec05-F11","sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, turning rules apply everywhere you turn, including driveways and alleys. After you stop and yield, may you go?","fact_ids":["sec05-F19"]},"answer":{"text":"Yes. A turn from a two-way road onto a one-way road may be made on red after stopping and yielding.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19","sec05-R07"]},"rationale":{"text":"The road you enter is one-way, so the red-light turn is allowed once you have stopped and yielded to traffic and pedestrians.","fact_ids":["sec05-F19","sec05-R07"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Lining up every turn","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Right turns start at the curb.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-R06"]},{"text":"Left turns start beside the center line.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-R06"]},{"text":"Some turns are allowed on red.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about lining your car up correctly for a turn and knowing when a red light still lets you go. Where you start depends on the direction you are turning, and where you end depends on the kind of road you enter. We will begin with right turns and left turns on two-way roads, including the head check that comes before both. Then we will look at the three combinations of one-way and two-way roads, and finish with the question test writers love: which turns may be made against a red light after you stop, and which may never be made on red. Keep the road you are entering in mind throughout.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The right turn setup","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R05","sec05-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Get as close as you can to the right curb.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R05","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Or to the right road edge.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R05","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Look left, ahead, right, then left again.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R05","sec05-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"For a right turn, move as close as you can to the right curb, or to the edge of the road if there is no curb.
